title: How to Stop Procrastinating by Using the Two-Minute Rule
coreMove: Shrink a stalled habit to a two-minute entry ritual you cannot reasonably refuse, and protect that version before trying to grow it.

exampleSpecs.domain: a pediatric ICU nurse trying to start a journaling practice after twelve-hour shifts
exampleSpecs.audience: a shift worker whose evenings are wrecked by fatigue
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether she processes a hard week or carries it into the next one
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she narrows the habit from 'journal for twenty minutes' to 'open the notebook and write the date,' then stops there on purpose for the first two weeks

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance illustrator who keeps abandoning a personal portfolio site after the first hour
exampleSpecs.audience: a creative who treats every entry as a full session or nothing
exampleSpecs.stakes: a year of unfinished drafts and no public work to point clients to
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the before shows her opening Figma and immediately scoping a redesign; the after shows her ritual being 'place laptop on desk, open the file, close it' for ten days running

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school orchestra teacher trying to rebuild a daily violin practice he abandoned in grad school
exampleSpecs.audience: a former expert who is embarrassed to be a beginner at his own instrument again
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether he models for his students the practice he preaches, or quietly stops touching the instrument
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he catches himself about to do a 'real' forty-five-minute session on day three and consciously chooses to put the violin down after two minutes to keep the entry version sacred

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional sales manager who wants to read industry reports instead of scrolling at night
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who keeps buying books and not opening them
exampleSpecs.stakes: a creeping sense that her edge is dulling while younger reps quote sources she has not read
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: in conversation with her partner she defends 'reading one paragraph' as a complete success and resists his suggestion to 'just do a chapter while you're at it'

exampleSpecs.domain: a recently retired civil engineer trying to resume a swimming routine after a shoulder surgery
exampleSpecs.audience: a sixty-eight-year-old whose body punishes ambition
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether he stays mobile into his seventies or lets the pool become another thing he used to do
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the entry ritual is 'put on the swim trunks and drive to the pool'; some days he turns around in the parking lot, and the chapter treats that as a win, not a failure

exampleSpecs.domain: a line cook learning to meditate to manage pre-service anxiety
exampleSpecs.audience: someone whose workplace offers zero quiet time
exampleSpecs.stakes: panic attacks during dinner rush that he has started hiding from his sous chef
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he tests two versions of the habit in his head — a ten-minute morning sit he never does, and a single conscious breath before tying his apron — and notices which one he could still be doing in six months
